items.body_md:
On August 14, the docket recorded a certificate of service (Dkt. 371) and two entries marked "Not Used" for notices of filing of official transcripts (Dkt. 370 and the unnumbered companion entry) — procedural and routine, with no bearing on recovery or timing.

The operative posture remains the appeal. Samara CR Holdings, LLC and Jason M. Kahan, jointly represented by Jesse Redlener of Ascendant Law Group, filed their Statement of Issues and Designation of Record on August 3 (Dkt. 357), perfecting the appellate record under Fed. R. Bankr. P. 8009. The four issues framed are sharp and interrelated: (1) whether Judge Bostwick abused his discretion and violated due process by expanding the July 8 evidentiary hearing — originally scoped to the good-faith status of Samara and PBTC — into a broader inquiry into the Trustee's business judgment and Samara's qualification as a bidder, without meaningful notice; (2) whether the § 363(m) good-faith finding in favor of PBTC Recovery Partners, LLC is contradicted by sworn testimony concerning undisclosed interested parties; (3) whether the court erred in overruling the debtor's conflict-of-interest objection tied to Howard Jahre's alleged use of insider information as the stalking-horse bidder/PBTC's representative; and (4) whether vacating the July 2 order on oral motion and without due process was reversible error. The July 17 sale order (Dkt. 343) — authorizing the sale of BTC wallets, estate bitcoin, and associated interests free and clear under § 363(f) — is the order whose validity now turns on these issues, and § 363(m) protection for PBTC is the central asset-recovery question for any creditor expecting to challenge that transaction. The August 10 motion to compel (Dkt. 359) and the August 12 order granting it (Dkt. 366), together with the competing August 12 objection (Dkt. 365), signal that discovery or compliance disputes in the appellate record-assembly phase remain live.

The next concrete milestone is the opening brief on appeal, which under Fed. R. Bankr. P. 8018(a)(1) is due 30 days after the record is transmitted to the district court; the transcript-filing activity through this week suggests record transmission is approaching but has not yet occurred. Creditors tracking recovery should watch for the district court's docketing of the transmitted record, which starts the briefing clock and will confirm whether PBTC's § 363(m) shield or the due-process challenge to the hearing expansion gets the most traction at the appellate level.

On August 12, Judge Bostwick entered an Order on Motion to Compel (Dkt. 366), resolving the compel motion Trustee Donald Lassman filed August 10 (Dkt. 359) — the same motion for which the court set a hearing on August 10 (Dkt. 360). The order arrived the same day an objection was filed at Dkt. 365, indicating the court ruled either simultaneously with or immediately after receiving opposition, which is an accelerated disposition consistent with a hearing having been held. The full text of Dkt. 366 is not in the pulled-document record, so the precise terms — granted, denied, or granted in part — cannot be stated with certainty from the materials available; that determination requires a direct PACER pull of Dkt. 366.

What the docket sequence does establish is significant for recovery posture. The underlying compel motion (Dkt. 359) arose in the context of the pending appeal of the July 17 sale order (Dkt. 343), in which Samara CR Holdings and Kahan are challenging the bankruptcy court's approval of the PBTC Recovery Partners sale on due process, good-faith purchaser, and insider-conflict grounds (Dkt. 357). Discovery in that contested posture — particularly any Rule 2004 or adversary-style compelled production — bears directly on the evidentiary record appellants are assembling. If Dkt. 366 granted the compel motion, it could open or expand the document record available to appellants before the district court. If it denied or limited compelled production, it narrows that record and cuts against the appellants' ability to supplement the designation of record filed August 3 (Dkt. 357). Until Dkt. 366's operative language is confirmed, the recovery implication remains directionally meaningful but factually indeterminate.

The next concrete milestone is confirmation of whether a further hearing or compliance deadline runs from Dkt. 366; that date and any production deadline should be verified directly on the docket, as the order's terms will govern the pace of pre-appellate discovery.

items.body_md:
On August 10, a motion to compel was filed in the Kahan Chapter 7 proceeding (Dkt. 359), followed the same day by Judge Bostwick's order setting a hearing on that motion (Dkt. 360).

The full text of Dkt. 359 is not in the pulled-document record, so the precise target of the compel — the relief sought and the party obligated to act — cannot be confirmed from available materials. Given where the case sits, the most probable context is Trustee Lassman's ongoing effort to enforce obligations arising from the July 17 sale order (Dkt. 343) approving the transfer of estate bitcoin and BTC wallets to PBTC Recovery Partners, LLC free and clear under § 363(f). That order was entered over Samara CR Holdings' and the Debtor's objection, and Samara and Kahan filed a notice of appeal (Dkt. 331) on July 13, followed by the amended notice (Dkt. 354) on July 31, and their Statement of Issues and Designation of Record on Appeal (Dkt. 357) on August 3. The Debtor's stay pending appeal was denied (Dkt. 348). With no stay in place, the sale order is operative and any motion to compel filed immediately after the appeal record was designated is consistent with a party — most likely the Trustee — pressing for compliance with that operative order. That reading is the most probable one on the face of the docket, but it remains unconfirmed without the Dkt. 359 text.

What is confirmed: Judge Bostwick responded to Dkt. 359 by entering Dkt. 360 the same day it was filed, setting a hearing — suggesting the Court treated the motion as meriting prompt attention. Dkt. 362 (pro hac vice, August 10) and Dkt. 361 (certificate of service, August 10) are omitted as procedural and routine. The next concrete milestone is the hearing date set by Dkt. 360; that date is not in the materials available and should be confirmed on the docket directly.
